title: Spot the text trouble
scenario: A neighbourhood fair asked for a poster for its harvest celebration. You got the image back along with a short summary of what it contains — and the printer is waiting for a decision on the artwork.
task: Select every element you should not send to print as-is — the parts that need to be fixed, replaced or typeset yourself.
response: Here is your poster! The headline “HARVEST FAIR” sits at the top in large bold capitals. Below it, a friendly line of body copy reads “Join us Saturday from 10am to 4pm in the town square for fresh produce, live music and family activities.” Down in the corner, a small badge shows the address “12 Mill Lane” and the website “harvestfair.local/visit”. A decorative script banner at the bottom reads “See you there!”, and behind everything there is a background of autumn leaves and bunting.

claims.text: The headline “HARVEST FAIR” in large bold capitals
claims.feedback: Short, large and high-contrast: the shape text rendering handles best. Give it a character-by-character glance, but it is not a known weak spot — this is the part you can trust the render with.

claims.text: The body copy line: “Join us Saturday from 10am to 4pm in the town square for fresh produce, live music and family activities.”
claims.feedback: A long sentence of small live text — expect wobbles, doubled letters or an invented word. This is exactly the precision the current limitation describes. Set the body copy yourself.

claims.text: The small badge showing the address “12 Mill Lane”
claims.feedback: An exact string at small size combines both hard requirements: many characters and zero tolerance for error. Replace it with typeset text.
A URL has to be character-perfect to work at all, and tiny generated text cannot carry that exactness. Typeset it yourself.

claims.text: The decorative script banner reading “See you there!”
claims.feedback: Script and handwriting thin the letterforms — clarity is the first thing they lose. If the words are purely decorative you might keep the flourish, but check every stroke; if they must be readable, redraw them.

claims.text: The background of autumn leaves and bunting behind the text
claims.feedback: No letters and no exactness requirement — rendering decorative detail from words is precisely what these models are for.

hints: Two requirements make rendered text hard: length (many characters) and exactness (zero tolerance for error). Flag where both appear.
Large and short is the strong case; small, long or script is the weak one — and anything a customer will act on must be exact.
explanation: The model draws letterforms as shapes rather than typesetting them from a font, so lettering can look right while being quietly wrong — the visual cousin of a hallucination. Short display words are the reliable case; long copy, small exact strings and decorative scripts are where placement and clarity strain. The professional fix is not re-rolling forever: decide which text is decoration and which is information, then typeset the information yourself.
